summary: A dense Uwe Rosenberg building-and-engine game where players buy hexes, erect production buildings, and chain resource conversions to churn out high-value goods like whiskey, bricks, and relics. It plays like a heavier, more interlocking cousin of Agricola/Le Havre with less randomness and more spatial puzzle-solving about where buildings go.
praised: Strong replayability via the alternate Ireland/religious building sets
criticised: Long downtime in multiplayer, especially with 4
Steep learning curve and rulebook complexity
Can feel solitaire-ish with little direct interaction

interaction.kind: racing to claim limited building tiles from a shared supply
interaction.detail: Each player runs their own engine on their own board, but many building types exist in limited copies in a shared pool, so building one before an opponent denies them that option. Beyond that scarcity race, there is no direct attack, blocking of opponents' boards, or negotiation — most of the turn is spent optimizing your own tableau.
interaction.said: Commonly described alongside Rosenberg's other 'farming' games as largely solitaire-ish, but with a recurring note that the shared pool of building tiles creates a race — 'grab the good buildings before someone else does' rather than direct confrontation.

sources: remaining raw goods converted via table (peat, clay, grain, wood)
remaining refined goods (bricks, glass, ceramics, books, whiskey, etc.)
scoring.how_you_win: Place workers each round to build and operate production buildings on your bog/grove tiles; the player whose buildings and leftover goods convert to the most points when the fixed number of rounds ends wins.
scoring.score_note: scales up with fewer players (longer game)
